claims.claim: Social contract theory is the view that persons' moral and political obligations are dependent upon a contract or agreement among them to form the society in which they live.

The modern social contract tradition is standardly traced from Thomas Hobbes, who gave the first full exposition and defense, through John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and was revived in the twentieth century by John Rawls.

Hobbes argued from a hypothetical state of nature that life without common government is a condition of constant insecurity and fear of violent death, which he described as solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, and he presented a sovereign with authority to enforce peace as the remedy.

Locke's political philosophy centers on natural rights to life, liberty, and property that hold independently of any particular society's laws; legitimate government is based on consent, is limited in power, and may be resisted when it violates people's rights.

Rousseau's account centers on the general will, created through agreement with other free and equal persons and directed at the common good, and holds that citizens gain freedom through membership by obeying laws they collectively give themselves.

Social contract reasoning is usually presented as a hypothetical model concerned with public justification, asking what arrangements people could reasonably accept, rather than as a claim that an actual historical agreement occurred.

Rawls's justice as fairness uses the original position, whose main distinguishing feature is the veil of ignorance, in which parties choose principles without knowing their own personal characteristics, conceptions of the good, or social and historical circumstances.

Standard objections to social contract theory include that the contract is a fiction and a hypothetical agreement cannot bind any actual person, that consent is assumed rather than genuinely given by most people, and that the membership of the contracting parties is contested because animals and future generations are difficult to include in a consent-based model.

Political philosophy investigates questions of legitimacy in political institutions, and social contract theory is one influential account of when political authority is legitimate and worthy of loyalty.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the social contract should be read as a historical event or as a hypothetical model.
positions: Historical readings treat the contract as an actual agreement that grounds political obligation.
Most contemporary defenders treat the contract as a hypothetical model for public justification, while critics reply that a hypothetical agreement cannot bind actual persons.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both readings, explains that the hypothetical reading dominates contemporary work, and keeps explanation separate from endorsement.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Hobbes's pessimistic account of the state of nature is accurate.
positions: Hobbes argued that without common government people face constant insecurity and fear of violent death.
Critics dispute the psychology behind the picture and the claim that life without government must amount to a war of all against all; scholars also interpret Hobbes's view in different ways.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the account to Hobbes, notes that it is contested, and does not adjudicate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether Rousseau's account of freedom through the general will preserves individual freedom.
positions: Rousseau held that citizens are free by obeying laws they collectively give themselves.
His statement that those who reject the general will must be forced to be free is widely contested.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports Rousseau's view and the contested passage neutrally, without endorsing or condemning it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who belongs among the parties to the social contract.
positions: Consent-based models fit people who can consent and bargain.

Critics argue animals, children, and future generations are thereby excluded despite being affected; feminist and race-conscious critics argue the model may assume a narrow class of contracting parties.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports these as live objections rather than settling them.

sourceRecords.title: Contemporary Approaches to the Social Contract
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Tier A scholarly reference. Supports the lineage from Hobbes through Locke, Rousseau, and Kant to Rawls; the aim of public justification; the reliance of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on consent; the hypothetical character of the modern contract and the point that a hypothetical agreement cannot bind any actual person; and the original position and veil of ignorance. Facts synthesized in original prose; no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Locke's Political Philosophy
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Tier A scholarly reference. Supports Locke's natural rights to life, liberty, and property as independent of any particular society's laws; the state of nature as life according to reason without a common superior; express and tacit consent; legitimate government based on consent with separation of powers; and resistance when government attempts to take away people's rights. Original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Original Position
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Tier A scholarly reference. Supports the original position as a central feature of Rawls's justice as fairness, the veil of ignorance depriving parties of knowledge of personal characteristics and social and historical circumstances, and the contested boundary questions about concern for others, animals, and future generations. Facts synthesized; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Social Contract Theory
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Tier B scholarly reference. Supports the definition of social contract theory as the view that moral and political obligations depend on an agreement among persons; Hobbes's first full exposition and defense and his hypothetical state of nature; Locke; Rousseau's general will and the 'forced to be free' passage; Rawls's twentieth-century revival; and feminist and race-conscious criticisms. Original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Leviathan (Thomas Hobbes, 1651)
